# Thread Local Variables

`ThreadLocal<T>` associates a value with the current thread, allowing methods in
a call chain to access context without passing it as a parameter. This can
simplify a call chain, but makes the dependency less visible and does not
propagate context to another thread. The example compares it with explicitly
passing a request message.

The program also contrasts a shared `Random` with `ThreadLocalRandom`, a
pseudorandom generator for the current thread. This is a related use of
thread-local state, not a measurement of performance.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- explain how thread-local values differ from explicitly passed context;
- describe why pooled workers need request context removed after each task;
- distinguish thread-local slots from the objects they reference; and
- choose between shared `Random` and `ThreadLocalRandom` for the use case.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8) JDK
or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in your shell.

## The program to inspect

`Main` runs both demonstrations in sequence.

```java
package demo;

import static demo.utils.Logs.logHeaderAndJavaVersion;
import static demo.utils.Logs.logSection;

public final class Main {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        logHeaderAndJavaVersion("Thread Local");

        logSection("ThreadLocal example");
        ThreadLocalExample.run();

        logSection("ThreadLocalRandom example");
        ThreadLocalRandomExample.run();
    }
}
```

`ThreadLocalExample` first passes Alice’s and Bob’s messages through a call
chain explicitly. It then submits two tasks to a fixed pool. Each task sets its
current worker’s `REQUEST_MESSAGE`, reads it through a no-argument call chain,
and removes it in `finally`. Each thread has its own slot, but the values can
still refer to the same mutable object; `ThreadLocal` does not make such an
object thread-safe or provide synchronisation for shared state.

The later task is scheduled only after both request tasks complete. On normal
completion it runs on a pool worker and reads `NO REQUEST MESSAGE`: either the
worker’s value was removed or it had no value yet. `get()` initialises a new
value after removal. Without cleanup, a reused worker could retain a previous
request’s value and expose it to a later task; long-lived threads can also
retain values longer than intended. Removing a value does not close a resource
it refers to, so resource ownership and cleanup still matter.

The Java Memory Model (JMM) governs visibility and ordering of shared state.
`ThreadLocal` isolates the slots; it is not a publication mechanism for sharing
their values. Task submission through `ExecutorService` provides its documented
happens-before relationship from actions before submission to actions in that
task. The `allOf` completion stage orders the later task after both request
tasks; it does not transfer their thread-local values. Log order among
concurrent tasks depends on scheduling and is not evidence of a JMM guarantee.
The pool is shut down in `finally`.

```java
package demo;

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;

public final class ThreadLocalExample {

    private static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_MESSAGE = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> "NO REQUEST MESSAGE");

    public static void run() {
        log("Without ThreadLocal, every method in the call chain needs the request context");
        log("Alice received the message: '" + passThroughVariableWhichIsNeededByAnotherMethodMethodA("Message from Alice") + '\'');
        log("Bob received the message: '" + passThroughVariableWhichIsNeededByAnotherMethodMethodA("Message from Bob") + '\'');

        /* Only in Java 19 the ExecutorService implements AutoClosable! */
        final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        try {
            final CompletableFuture<Void> alice = CompletableFuture.runAsync(
                    () -> logReceivedMessage("Alice", "Message from Alice"), executor);

            final CompletableFuture<Void> bob = CompletableFuture.runAsync(
                    () -> logReceivedMessage("Bob", "Message from Bob"), executor);

            final CompletableFuture<Void> noRequest = CompletableFuture.allOf(alice, bob)
                    .thenRunAsync(() -> log("Later task received the message: '"
                            + callMethodThatReadFromThreadLocalMethodA() + '\''), executor);

            /* Wait for every task to complete */
            CompletableFuture.allOf(alice, bob, noRequest).join();
        } finally {
            executor.shutdown();
        }

        log("Done");
    }

    private static void logReceivedMessage(final String name, final String message) {
        REQUEST_MESSAGE.set(message);
        try {
            final String received = callMethodThatReadFromThreadLocalMethodA();
            log(name + " received the message: '" + received + '\'');
        } finally {
            REQUEST_MESSAGE.remove();
        }
    }

    private static String passThroughVariableWhichIsNeededByAnotherMethodMethodA(final String message) {
        return passThroughVariableWhichIsNeededByAnotherMethodMethodB(message);
    }

    private static String passThroughVariableWhichIsNeededByAnotherMethodMethodB(final String message) {
        return requiresTheVariableMethodC(message);
    }

    private static String requiresTheVariableMethodC(final String message) {
        return message;
    }

    private static String callMethodThatReadFromThreadLocalMethodA() {
        return callMethodThatReadFromThreadLocalMethodB();
    }

    private static String callMethodThatReadFromThreadLocalMethodB() {
        return readsFromThreadLocalMethodC();
    }

    private static String readsFromThreadLocalMethodC() {
        /* Get the message from the ThreadLocal */
        return REQUEST_MESSAGE.get();
    }
}
```

`ThreadLocalRandomExample` first has both tasks use one shared `Random`, then
calls `ThreadLocalRandom.current()` from each task. `Random` is thread-safe, but
concurrent use of one instance can encounter contention. A `ThreadLocalRandom`
is isolated to the current thread and can reduce that contention; the printed
values do not measure throughput. Use a benchmark such as JMH for a
workload-specific comparison.

Neither generator is cryptographically secure; use `SecureRandom` for
security-sensitive applications. For a reproducible sequence, use a `Random`
with a defined seed and the same sequence of calls. Concurrent scheduling can
change which task receives each value from a shared generator. Per-thread
caching is another possible use of `ThreadLocal`, but avoid it for data that
must be shared between threads and consider the lifetime of cached resources.

```java
package demo;

import java.util.Random;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.function.IntSupplier;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;

public final class ThreadLocalRandomExample {

    private static final Random SHARED_RANDOM = new Random();

    public static void run() {
        final int numberOfWorkers = 2;

        /* Only in Java 19 the ExecutorService implements AutoClosable! */
        final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(numberOfWorkers);
        try {
            log("A shared Random is thread-safe, but both workers update one generator");
            generateRandomNumbers(executor, "Shared Random", () -> SHARED_RANDOM.nextInt(100) + 1, numberOfWorkers);

            log("ThreadLocalRandom gives each worker random state without sharing this generator");
            generateRandomNumbers(executor, "ThreadLocalRandom",
                    () -> ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 101), numberOfWorkers);
        } finally {
            executor.shutdown();
        }

        log("Done");
    }

    private static void generateRandomNumbers(final ExecutorService executor,
                                              final String generatorName,
                                              final IntSupplier nextRandomNumber,
                                              final int numberOfWorkers) {
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                        IntStream.range(0, numberOfWorkers)
                                .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
                                    final int randomNumber = nextRandomNumber.getAsInt();
                                    log(generatorName + " generated random number: " + randomNumber);
                                }, executor))
                                .toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
                .join();
    }
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from the `examples/thread-local-variables` directory. Choose
one of the following ways to run the example. Observe the request messages and
later default value; the order of concurrent output and the random values vary.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

